column1: When is P IMPLIES Q false? Write it in code.
column2: Only when P is true and Q is false. In code: !p || q.
… the if-part is false or the then-part is true (MCS §3.1.3, p. 50).

column1: Why is an implication with a false hypothesis counted as true?
column2: A promise that wasn't triggered isn't broken. E.g. a 12-rule spec where only 2 sensors fired must still come out true. Same idea as all([]) == True.

column1: Is OR inclusive or exclusive in maths? Which operator is 'exactly one'?
column2: Inclusive: P OR Q is true when both are. 'Exactly one' is XOR (p != q on bools).
x > 0 || y > 100. A OR (NOT A AND B) ≡ A OR B (MCS §3.2, pp. 52–53).

column1: Contrapositive vs converse of P IMPLIES Q. Which is equivalent?
column2: Contrapositive NOT(Q) ⇒ NOT(P): equivalent. Converse Q ⇒ P: not equivalent (differs when exactly one of P, Q is true).

column1: Wason cards A, K, 4, 7. Rule: vowel ⇒ even on the back. Which must you turn?
column2: A and 7. Only a vowel with an odd number can break it. K: if-part false. 4: then-part already true.

column1: What's the 'inverse' NOT(P) ⇒ NOT(Q) equivalent to?
column2: The converse Q ⇒ P, not the original. A common wrong 'contrapositive': you must negate AND swap.

column1: Valid vs satisfiable, in truth-table terms
column2: Valid: every row is T. Satisfiable: at least one row is T (MCS §3.3.2, p. 56).
